Plaintiff’s strategy of repeatedly seeking to amend his complaint, delaying resolution of
his claims, and wasting the resources of both the court and the parties, has continued in this action.
Plaintiff first brought the claims he raises in the instant action against Defendants NCMEC and
Katie Hall (together, the “NCMEC Defendants) in a separate action, Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for
Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-1341 (E.D. Va.). In that action, Plaintiff sought leave
to amend his complaint to add claims against Meta. After the NCMEC Defendants opposed that
request, Plaintiff voluntarily dismissed that action, re-asserting his claims in the instant action one
day later. See Dkt. No. 1. Plaintiff filed his FAC shortly thereafter (Dkt. No. 5), and each Defendant
moved to dismiss the FAC. See Dkt. Nos. 10, 21, 45.
Following Defendants’ briefing on the Motions to Dismiss, Plaintiff sought leave to amend
his complaint in the instant matter three additional times, including the instant motion. See Dkt.
Nos. 26, 59, 114. Plaintiff withdrew his first request for leave to amend after Meta’s Opposition
noted that Plaintiff failed to attach a copy of his proposed amended complaint to his motion. See
Dkt. Nos. 53, 57. After Plaintiff filed his second request for leave to amend (Dkt. No. 59), the
Court ordered Plaintiff to “provide a redlined version of the Amended Complaint” in order to
provide the Court with “sufficient information to issue an order on this matter.” Dkt. No. 64.
Plaintiff failed to comply with that order, and the Court denied his second motion. Dkt. No. 84.
Plaintiff now seeks leave to amend for a third time, reiterating many of the allegations in
Plaintiff’s prior proposed amendments against Meta and the NCMEC Defendants. See Dkt. No.
114.1 Plaintiff also seeks to add a new proposed defendant, Panayiota Souras, who Plaintiff alleges
1

seeking a variety of relief, in a transparent effort to drive up litigation costs to attempt to coerce a
settlement. See Dkt. Nos. 109-135; see also Dkt. No. 133 (Plaintiff asserting that “an early
settlement conference” may be appropriate “[g]iven the number and scope of the pending
proceedings”).

is the “Chief Legal Officer of NCMEC.” Dkt. No. 114-2, Second Amended Complaint, (“SAC”)

II.
PLAINTIFF’S PROPOSED SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT IS FUTILE.
“[T]he standards used by a district court in ruling on a motion to amend or on a motion to
supplement [a complaint] are nearly identical.” Franks v. Ross, 313 F.3d 184, 198, n. 15 (4th Cir.
2002). In either case, “leave to amend a pleading should be denied. . . when the amendment would
be futile.” Brannen v. Selene Finance, LP, No. 2:18-cv-602, 2019 WL 13251099, at *2, 5 (E.D.
Va. Nov. 14, 2019) (denying leave to file supplemental complaint where “it would be futile to
permit” Plaintiff’s “supplemental pleading” where his “right to relief” remained “a matter of pure
speculation”); see also Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. N.C. DOT, 914 F.3d 213, 228 (4th Cir. 2019)
(holding a proposed amendment is futile “when it is clearly insufficient or frivolous on its
face…[or] if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss.”).
As to Plaintiff’s supplemental allegations regarding the NCMEC Defendants, including the
proposed addition of NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer as a defendant, Meta fully adopts the
arguments in NCMEC’s Opposition, which explain why the supplemental allegations are “futile
and unnecessary.” Dkt. No. 139 at 4-6.
Nor do Plaintiff’s proposed supplemental allegations as to Meta save his failed claims.
First, the proposed SAC alleges that because Meta mentioned this case in its motion to dismiss a
separate action that Plaintiff brought against Meta in the Northern District of California (Ballentine
v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-05939-RFL (N.D. Cal.)), “[b]y August 13, 2026, Meta had
actual knowledge that this action exists” and therefore the “August 13, 2026 filing is alleged as a
subsequent fact bearing on Meta’s knowledge, position, coordination, and litigation context.” SAC
¶¶ 184-185. But Plaintiff acknowledges that “[n]o claim for relief rests on” this proposed new

allegation regarding Meta. Id. ¶ 185. And, as Meta explained in its previous opposition to
Plaintiff’s request to amend (Dkt. No. 53), Meta’s knowledge that Plaintiff sued NCMEC as of
August 13, 2026 has no relevance whatsoever to Plaintiff’s claims against Meta, which are
premised on Plaintiff’s assertion that Meta somehow conspired with NCMEC in connection with
letters that NCMEC sent to Plaintiff on April 22, 2026. Indeed, Plaintiff now acknowledges that
“no claim rests on” this proposed supplemental allegation. Dkt. No. 115 at 13. Because Plaintiff’s
newly added allegations against Meta are plainly irrelevant to his claims or the issues raised in
Meta’s motion to dismiss, amendment would be futile and Plaintiff’s motion should be denied. See
Porter v. Blue Ridge Bankshares, Inc.¸ No. 3:24-cv-909, 2025 WL 2025356, at *5, n.4 (E.D. Va.
July 18, 2025) (denying leave to amend as futile where “the proposed amended complaint does
not change the Court’s analysis regarding Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss”); Dacha v. Moody, No.
3:24-cv-713, 2026 WL 625494, at *15 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2026) (denying motion to supplement
under Rule 15(d) because “[p]ermitting [plaintiff] to supplement the records with the facts”
identified in the motion to supplement “would be futile” where the facts could not plausibly serve
“as a factual basis for any claim” against defendants).
Second, Plaintiff also suggests that the fact that NCMEC’s Chief Legal Officer was
employed at Orrick (which represents Meta in this action) twenty years ago supports his conspiracy
theory. See SAC ¶ 96. It does not. Nowhere does Plaintiff allege, in any non-conclusory fashion,
that Ms. Souras had any contact with Meta regarding the subject matter of any of his claims.
Instead, the proposed SAC alleges only that Ms. Souras participated in the purported conspiracy
by participating in drafting the response to Plaintiff’s proposed subpoena through her role at
NCMEC. SAC ¶ 154. The mere allegation that Ms. Souras worked at Orrick twenty years prior to
the events at issue does not and cannot give rise to any plausible inference of conspiracy.
